items.title: Twenty Obstacles Reduce to Four Causes — and "Attaining Concentration" Closes

items.zh: 又此二十種所對治法，略由四相，於所生起三摩地中，堪能為障。何等為四？一、於三摩地方便不善巧故；二、於一切修定方便全無加行故；三、顛倒加行故；四、加行縵緩故。
items.en: These twenty things to be remedied can, in brief, obstruct the arising of concentration through four causes. What are the four? Lacking skill in the means of concentration; making no effort towards it at all; applying effort in a mistaken way; and applying effort too slowly and half-heartedly.

items.zh: 此三摩地所對治法，有二十種白法對治；與此相違，應知其相。由此能斷所對治法，多所作故；疾疾能得正住其心，證三摩地。又得此三摩地，當知即是得初靜慮近分定未至位所攝。又此得三摩地相違法，及得三摩地隨順法廣聖教義，當知唯有此二十種。除此更無若過若增。由此因緣，依初世間一切種清淨，於此正法補特伽羅得三摩地，已善宣說、已善開示。
items.en: For these twenty things that hinder concentration there are twenty bright remedies; their characteristics should be understood as the opposite of these. By them one is able to cut off the things to be remedied; and because much is done in this way, one very swiftly succeeds in settling the mind correctly and attaining concentration. Further, it should be understood that attaining this concentration belongs to the not-yet-arrived stage, the preliminary access to the first meditative absorption. Further, the meaning of the noble teaching in full concerning what is contrary to attaining concentration and what is conducive to it should be understood to consist only of these twenty kinds. Beyond this, there is nothing further to exceed it, and nothing further to add. For this reason, under the first heading of mundane purity of every kind, the attainment of concentration by a person within this true teaching has been well declared and well revealed.

items.title: Perfecting Concentration: Ten Marks on the Way to the First Absorption and Beyond

items.zh: 復次，如是已得三摩地者，於此少小殊勝定中，不生喜足。於勝三摩地圓滿，更起求願。
items.en: Further, one who has attained concentration does not rest content with this small measure of excellence, but arouses a further aspiration towards the perfection of superior concentration.

items.zh: 又即於彼見勝功德。又由求願見勝功德，為求彼故；勇猛精進，策勵而住。又彼於色相應愛味俱行煩惱，非能一切皆永斷故，名非得勝。又非於彼諸善法中皆勤修故，名他所勝。又於廣大淨天生處，無有沈沒。又彼無能陵篾於己，下劣信解增上力故。又彼如是心無沈沒，於定所緣境界法中，即先所得止、舉、捨相，無間、殷重方便修故；隨順而轉。又彼如是隨法相轉，數入數出，為欲證得速疾通慧，依定圓滿，樂聞正法故；於時時中慇懃請問。又依如是三摩地圓滿故，於正方便根本定攝內心奢摩他，證得遠離愛樂。又證得法毘鉢舍那。如是觀察熾然明淨所有愛樂。當知齊此已能證入根本靜慮，如是名為三摩地圓滿。又此三摩地圓滿廣聖教義，當知唯有如是十相。除此更無若過若增。
items.en: Further, one sees surpassing good qualities in it. And because one aspires to and sees these surpassing good qualities, in order to seek them one dwells with courageous effort, spurring oneself on. Further, because the afflictions accompanying the relish of craving connected with form have not all been permanently cut off, this is called 'not having attained the surpassing'. And because one has not diligently cultivated all those wholesome qualities, this is called 'being surpassed by others'. Further, with regard to the vast places of rebirth among the pure gods, one does not lose heart. Further, one does not belittle oneself through the influence of a lowly conviction. Further, with the mind thus not losing heart, with regard to the phenomena that are the object of concentration — namely the signs of calm, exertion and equanimity previously obtained — because one cultivates them by uninterrupted and earnest means, one proceeds in conformity with them. Further, proceeding thus in accordance with the signs of the teaching, entering and emerging again and again, in order to attain swift, penetrating wisdom, relying on the perfecting of concentration and delighting in hearing the true teaching, one earnestly asks questions from time to time. Further, by relying on such perfecting of concentration, one attains delight in seclusion, the inner calm-abiding belonging to the root concentration of correct practice. And one attains insight into the teaching. One thus examines with delight that is blazing, bright and pure. It should be understood that at this point one is already able to enter the root meditative absorption. This is called perfecting concentration. Further, the meaning of the noble teaching in full concerning this perfecting of concentration should be understood to consist only of these ten aspects. Beyond this, there is nothing further to exceed it, and nothing further to add.

items.title: Mastery Opens: Even the Root Absorptions Still Carry Hidden Flaws

items.zh: 復次，雖已證得根本三摩地故，名三摩地圓滿；其心猶為三摩地生愛味、慢、見、疑、無明等諸隨煩惱之所染污，未名圓滿清淨鮮白。
items.en: Further, although one has already attained the root concentrations — called "perfecting concentration" — the mind may still be defiled by secondary afflictions arising in connection with that very concentration: craving for it, conceit over it, wrong views regarding it, doubt, and ignorance. Such attainment cannot yet be called complete, pure, and radiant.

items.zh: 為令如是諸隨煩惱不現行故，為練心故，為調心故，彼作是思：我應當證心自在性、定自在性。於四處所，以二十二相應善觀察。謂自誓受下劣形相、威儀、眾具；又自誓受禁制尸羅；又自誓受精勤無間修習善法。若有為斷一切苦惱，受此三處，應正觀察眾苦隨逐。由剃除鬚髮故，捨俗形好故，著壞色衣故，應自觀察形色異人。如是名為觀察誓受下劣形相。於行住坐臥語默等中，不隨欲行；制伏憍慢往趣他家，審正觀察遊行乞食。如是名為觀察誓受下劣威儀。又正觀察從他獲得無所畜積諸供身具，如是名為觀察誓受下劣眾具。由此五相，當知是名初處觀察。又善說法毘奈耶中，諸出家者所受尸羅，略捨二事之所顯現。一者、棄捨父母、妻子、奴婢、僕使、朋友、眷屬、財穀珍寶等所顯。二者、棄捨歌舞、倡伎、笑戲、歡娛、遊從、掉逸、親愛聚會，種種世事之所顯現。又彼安住尸羅律儀，不由犯戒私自懇責，亦不為彼同梵行者以法呵擯；有犯尸羅而不輕舉。若於尸羅有所缺犯，由此因緣，便自懇責；若同梵行以法呵擯，即便如法而自悔除。於能舉罪同梵行者，心無恚恨，無損無惱而自修治。由此五相，是名於第二處觀察。如是尸羅善圓滿已，應以五相精勤方便修諸善品。
items.en: So that these secondary afflictions do not occur, in order to train the mind and to tame the mind, one reflects thus: 'I should attain mastery of mind and mastery of concentration.' One examines well in four domains through twenty-two aspects. That is: one vows to take on a lowly appearance, deportment and requisites; one vows to take on the restraint of moral discipline; and one vows to take on the diligent, uninterrupted cultivation of wholesome qualities. One who takes on these three domains in order to cut off all suffering and vexation should correctly examine how one is followed by many sufferings. Because one has shaved off hair and beard, abandoned the fine appearance of lay life, and wears robes of a discoloured hue, one should examine how one's appearance differs from that of others. This is called examining one's vow to take on a lowly appearance. In walking, standing, sitting, lying, speaking and keeping silent, one does not act as one pleases; one subdues pride when going to the houses of others, and goes on the alms round with careful and correct examination. This is called examining one's vow to take on a lowly deportment. Further, one correctly examines that the requisites for supporting the body are obtained from others and that nothing is stored up. This is called examining one's vow to take on lowly requisites. By these five aspects, this should be understood as the examination of the first domain. Further, in the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya, the moral discipline taken on by those who have gone forth is displayed, in brief, by the abandoning of two things. First, it is displayed by the abandoning of father and mother, wife and children, servants and attendants, friends and relatives, wealth, grain, treasures and the like. Second, it is displayed by the abandoning of singing and dancing, entertainments, jokes and play, merriment, outings, restless excitement, affectionate gatherings, and all kinds of worldly affairs. Further, one dwells in the restraint of moral discipline: one does not privately reproach oneself for having broken a precept, nor is one rebuked and expelled in accordance with the Dharma by fellow practitioners of the holy life; and if one does transgress in moral discipline, one does not treat it lightly. If there is any lapse in moral discipline, one reproaches oneself on that account; if fellow practitioners of the holy life rebuke one in accordance with the Dharma, one at once makes amends through confession in accordance with the Dharma. Towards the fellow practitioners who raise the offence, one's mind harbours no resentment; without harming or troubling them, one corrects oneself. By these five aspects, this is called the examination of the second domain. Having thus brought moral discipline to good completion, one should diligently apply oneself to cultivating wholesome qualities through five aspects.

blocks.text: How the twenty obstacles reduce to four causes, how concentration is perfected, and the beginning of the long section on mastery. Several passages are **missing from Ru-Yi's translation**; the English column gives our own translation, marked as ours.

The twenty obstacles come down to four causes: lacking skill in the method; making no effort; making effort in the wrong way; making effort too slowly. Venerable Miào Jìng: practising insight when calm is needed, calm when insight is needed; insisting on walking when one should sit.

The prose missing from Ru-Yi's translation (0391b24): twenty contrary practices remedy the twenty obstacles, and with them one quickly settles the mind and attains concentration: the access stage of the first dhyāna (未至定).

One who has attained concentration "does not rest content with this small measure of excellence". Venerable Miào Jìng: "small" disparages access concentration; "excellence" still praises it, because it is not easy.

The prose missing from Ru-Yi's translation (0391c06) gives ten marks of perfecting: seeing the higher qualities; striving for them; recognising that the afflictions of the form realm are not yet cut ("not yet victorious") and that one has not practised every good ("surpassed by others"); not being discouraged by the vast purity of the higher heavens; not belittling oneself; practising the signs of calming, rousing, and equanimity continuously and earnestly; entering and emerging repeatedly; asking questions in order to gain swift higher knowledge; attaining the delight of seclusion in the root absorption; and the delight of clear insight. With these, one enters the root absorption.

Even in the root absorptions, the mind may be defiled by secondary afflictions arising from the concentration itself: craving for it, pride, views, doubt. Master Cháng Bǎi: free of affliction is "pure"; continuously liberated from it is "radiant".

(Missing from Ru-Yi's translation; the English column gives our own.) To train the mind for mastery, the renunciant reflects on four places in twenty-two ways. First, one has vowed to take a humble **appearance** (shaved head, dyed robes), humble **deportment** (not acting at will; going for alms without pride), and humble **requisites** (only what is given, nothing stored). Second, the **precepts**, which mean giving up family, wealth, and worldly amusements, and making amends at once when one falls short, without resentment towards the one who points it out.

quiz.q: By which four causes do the twenty obstacles hinder concentration?
options: unskilled in means, no effort, mistaken effort, slack effort
faults of teacher, friends, teaching, self
quiz.why: "Lacking skill in the means of concentration; making no effort at all; applying effort in a mistaken way; and applying effort too slowly." Venerable Miào Jìng: the twenty obstacles are the detailed account; these four are the summary.

quiz.q: How do the masters illustrate "mistaken effort" and "slack effort"?
options: Miào Jìng: doing insight when calm is needed, wandering when one should sit, sitting only half an hour; Cháng Bǎi: heating water to twenty degrees and stopping
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: when he should practise calm he does insight, when he should do insight he does calm; when he should sit he insists on running about. Master Cháng Bǎi: like boiling water that needs a hundred degrees, but he always stops at twenty — too slow.

quiz.q: How does the treatise say one who has attained concentration should regard this small excellence?
options: not rest content, but arouse a further aspiration towards perfecting superior concentration
quiz.why: "One who has attained concentration does not rest content with this small measure of excellence, but arouses a further aspiration towards the perfection of superior concentration." Venerable Miào Jìng: aspiration is the leader.

quiz.q: In "this small measure of excellence," what does Venerable Miào Jìng see in the phrase?
options: "small" disparages access concentration, while "excellence" still praises it, since it is hard to attain
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: "small" disparages access concentration; "excellence" still praises it, because it is not easy to attain. Master Cháng Bǎi: access concentration is hard to gain and easy to lose.

quiz.q: After attaining the root concentrations, why can it not yet be called "complete, pure, and radiant"?
options: the mind is still defiled by secondary afflictions arising from concentration — craving, conceit, views, doubt, ignorance
quiz.why: "The mind may still be defiled by secondary afflictions arising in connection with that very concentration: craving for it, conceit, wrong views, doubt, and ignorance. Such attainment cannot yet be called complete, pure, and radiant." Master Cháng Bǎi: being free of affliction is "pure"; continuous liberation from it is "radiant."

quiz.q: How does Master Cháng Bǎi distinguish "pure" from "radiant"?
options: being free of affliction is pure; continuous liberation from it is radiant
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: being far from affliction is called pure; continuously liberated from affliction is called radiant.
